# Nishon Notes: expanded machine-readable summary

Site: https://nishon.com.np/
Author: Nishon Tandukar
Language: English
Primary subjects: Geospatial software engineering in Nepal, GeoAI workflows, geospatial data pipelines, geoprocessing workflows, OpenStreetMap, spatial data infrastructure, Python, open data, humanitarian technology, and remote sensing.

## Author

Nishon Tandukar is a Geospatial Software Engineer based in Nepal and Director of Geospatial Intelligence at NAXA. He works on open-source geospatial systems, humanitarian mapping, spatial data infrastructure, geospatial data pipelines, and applied GeoAI. The blog is a public record of technical experiments, open-source projects, implementation decisions, limitations, and lessons from practice.

## Article: Kathmandu Valley Wallpapers: 1,898 Places of Worship

Canonical URL: https://nishon.com.np/city-of-temples-wallpapers
Published: 2026-11-01
License: CC BY 4.0. Required credit: Nishon Tandukar (nishon.com.np/city-of-temples-wallpapers). Map and place data © OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL 1.0 (openstreetmap.org/copyright). Terrain: SRTM and GMTED2010 data courtesy of the U.S. Geological Survey, via AWS Terrain Tiles.
Data sources: OpenStreetMap via the Overpass API (places of worship, shrines, stupas, district borders, roads), AWS Terrain Tiles (elevation)

Summary: Free light and dark phone (1440x3120) and desktop (3840x2160) wallpapers showing the 1,898 places of worship mapped in OpenStreetMap inside the Kathmandu, Lalitpur and Bhaktapur district borders (1,116 tagged Hindu, 282 Buddhist, the rest untagged). Each place is a dot over hard-edged colour steps of density, smoothed over about a kilometre. The count is a lower bound because OpenStreetMap only holds what has been mapped, and it includes shrines, stupas and a few churches and mosques.

## Article: Dashain Flights Wallpapers for Kathmandu and Pokhara

Canonical URL: https://nishon.com.np/dashain-flights-wallpapers
Published: 2026-10-23
License: CC BY 4.0. Required credit: Nishon Tandukar (nishon.com.np/dashain-flights-wallpapers). Flight data © adsb.lol and its feeders, ODbL 1.0. Map data © OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL 1.0 (openstreetmap.org/copyright). Terrain: SRTM and GMTED2010 data courtesy of the U.S. Geological Survey, via AWS Terrain Tiles.
Data sources: adsb.lol globe history (flights), OpenStreetMap (roads, towns, runways), AWS Terrain Tiles (elevation)

Summary: Free light and dark phone (1440x3120) and desktop (3840x2160) wallpapers showing every counted flight over Kathmandu (1,259 flights at Tribhuvan International Airport, VNKT) and Pokhara (195 flights at Pokhara International Airport) on the five Dashain days 17 to 21 October 2026. Fulpati, 17 October, was the busiest Kathmandu day with 278 flights. Red lines are Nepali (9N-registered, non-wide-body) flights and blue lines are foreign flights; darker means lower altitude. The final approach and take-off roll are modelled from runway geometry because ground receivers lose low aircraft in the Kathmandu valley, helicopters and distant overflights are excluded, and counts are a lower bound.

## Article: Building a Public Nepal Earthquake Dataset

Canonical URL: https://nishon.com.np/building-a-public-nepal-earthquake-dataset.html
Published: 2026-07-23
Source repository: https://github.com/konishon/nepal-earthquake-epicenter-data
Original data source: National Earthquake Monitoring and Research Center, Government of Nepal.

Summary: The article explains a Playwright and Beautiful Soup pipeline that extracts earthquake records published by Nepal's National Earthquake Monitoring and Research Center. Records include Bikram Sambat and Gregorian dates, local and UTC times, coordinates, magnitude, and epicenter. A SHA-256 identifier deduplicates normalized records. The project appends results to CSV and JSON and creates GeoJSON Point features for mapping. A weekly GitHub Actions workflow runs collection and commits updates. The article emphasizes that this is a secondary publication whose accuracy and completeness depend on the original source and on continued compatibility with the source website.

## Article: Finding Nepal's Local Level from a Coordinate

Canonical URL: https://nishon.com.np/finding-nepals-local-level-from-a-coordinate.html
Published: 2026-07-23
Source repository: https://github.com/konishon/nepal-palika-finder

Summary: The article explains a Python library for identifying the Nepali Gaupalika or Nagarpalika containing a latitude-longitude coordinate. The package bundles local-level polygons as FlatGeobuf, loads features through Fiona, and builds a Shapely STRtree. Each query first retrieves spatial candidates and then applies an exact point-in-polygon predicate. The library also supports prefix-based name search, district-assisted disambiguation, geometry retrieval, and enumeration of bundled features. The article notes that points exactly on boundaries need an explicit predicate policy and that operational users should verify the source, date, and completeness of the bundled administrative data.

## Article: Visualizing Pathfinding on OpenStreetMap

Canonical URL: https://nishon.com.np/visualizing-pathfinding-on-openstreetmap.html
Published: 2026-07-23
Source repository: https://github.com/konishon/osm-pathfinding-visualizer

Summary: The article describes a Python pathfinding visualizer that downloads drivable OpenStreetMap networks through OSMnx, projects them into metric coordinates, and compares Breadth-First Search, Dijkstra, A*, and Greedy Best-First Search. Traversal implementations yield explored edges, separating algorithm execution from rendering. Matplotlib displays the search and final route in 2D or 3D. Generated sine-wave audio provides search progress and a path-found signal. The application supports interactive viewing, static previews, GIF export, and MP4 export with audio.

## Article: Testing Semantic Change Detection with Aerial Image Captions

Canonical URL: https://nishon.com.np/reading-the-landscape-with-ai.html
Published: 2026-07-01

Summary: The article tests Moondream2 on two dates from a LEVIR-CD aerial-image pair. A small NLP pipeline compares sentence embeddings and extracts land-cover and land-use terms from separate captions. The resulting text suggests a shift from open land to built development, but it does not locate or measure change. Caption errors, guessed land use, limited keyword lists, and the loss of spatial detail prevent the method from serving as evidence on its own. The proposed next step is to connect model explanations to geometries produced by a conventional change-detection model and evaluate them against LEVIR-CD masks.

## Citation guidance

Use each article's canonical URL. When discussing source datasets or repositories, cite both the blog article and its linked primary repository. Do not treat experimental results as operational guarantees. Preserve the limitations described in each article.
